news.title: Why Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline matters for global oil
news.raw_text:
Why Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline matters for global oil
The 1,200km (745 mile) pipeline has been temporarily closed, affecting up to 5 percent of global oil supply.
In another blow to global oil markets, drones struck Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline last Thursday, prompting the kingdom to suspend operations.
The 1,200km (746-mile) pipeline, which carries roughly 4 to 5 million barrels of oil per day (bpd), links the country’s major oil-producing fields in the east with the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which has largely been closed since the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran in February.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said the shutdown was a “precautionary” measure after the attack caused damage and injuries in the Riyadh and Medina regions.
The closure comes as the US-Israel war on Iran has sharply reduced oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi forces in Yemen have intensified attacks around the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb.
With oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz severely disrupted, Saudi Arabia has relied more heavily on the East-West pipeline. What does its closure mean for an already tight global oil market?
How bad is the damage?
The extent of the damage is not yet clear, and estimates of how quickly the pipeline can return to normal operations vary. Sources familiar with the incident told the Reuters news agency that repairs could take five to six weeks, while another source said operations could restart sooner.
Saudi officials said drones hit the pipeline in two areas around Riyadh and Medina. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the attack caused injuries and damage to infrastructure.
According to Saudi authorities, the launch of the drones was traced to Maysan province in southeastern Iraq, close to the Iranian border and an area where Iran-aligned armed groups have established a longstanding presence.
The attack follows a strike in March near the Saudi-Aramco-ExxonMobil refinery in Yanbu that temporarily disrupted crude loadings from the Red Sea port. That incident had little lasting impact on operations, with shipments recovering within days, but it demonstrated that the kingdom’s western oil infrastructure was not immune to attacks.
What is the East-West pipeline?
The East-West pipeline, also known as the Petroline, is a 1,200km (745-mile) long oil pipeline built in 1981 that carries crude oil from the kingdom’s eastern oil fields near Abqaiq across the Arabian Peninsula to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
It has a maximum capacity of seven million bpd, although actual flows have been lower in recent months – about two million bpd in August according to Kpler – the lowest monthly level since January as Houthi attacks made the Red Sea route difficult to use.
Saudi Arabia increased the amount of crude sent west during the first five months of the conflict, taking flows to roughly 4-5 million bpd. That represents about 4 to 5 percent of global supply and allowed the world’s second largest oil exporter to bypass the Strait of Hormuz when shipping conditions deteriorated.
Why is it important?
The pipeline’s closure comes at a critical point for the global oil market.
Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz supplied more than a fifth of oil globally – about 20 million bpd. According to Reuters, industry estimates now put the flow at about 6-9 million bpd through the strait, a dramatic reduction in the volume.
Saudi Arabia has responded by moving more crude towards the Red Sea. However, the flow and export of that oil depends on the pipeline, storage facilities and tankers transiting safely – all of which have been made vulnerable since the Iran war began in February.
According to sources close to Reuters, if the pipeline remains shut, Yanbu has enough available stocks to sustain exports for about five to seven days, while Egyptian facilities in Ain Sukhna and Sidi Kerir, which store Saudi oil, could provide additional supplies for several days.
While this gives Saudi Arabia some buffer, it comes as global inventories have already been falling. The International Energy Agency said Saudi oil supply reached a more than three-decade low in August, with disruptions in Hormuz and the Red Sea. It says world oil supplies will decline by some 5.7 million bpd this year, equivalent to 6 percent of global supply.
Oil prices have so far been cushioned by stockpiles and releases from strategic reserves, with Brent crude trading about $70-$90 in recent months. But the longer regional disruptions continue, the more those reserves will be depleted and the higher prices will rise.
In June, the IEA said continued drawdowns could hit critical levels with experts saying that if inventories approach exceptionally low levels, Brent could potentially rise to $150 a barrel.
If damage to the pipeline proves extensive, and attacks continue to threaten Yanbu and shipping routes beyond it, Saudi Arabia could find that its ability to compensate for lost Gulf exports is itself becoming constrained.
Gavekal Research noted that if Yanbu, which processes more than one million bpd, goes offline because of threats from Houthi drones, “this would be a disaster for the world at a time when global refining capacity is already critically tight.”

news.title: Temporary Hormuz solution deferred as Iran-Arab summit falls through
news.raw_text:
Temporary Hormuz solution deferred as Iran-Arab summit falls through
Saudi Arabia asked for the meeting to be postponed, but Tehran says it will continue to seek a regionally backed bill.
Tehran, Iran – Another attempt to clinch a deal between Iran and Oman to restore some traffic to the Strait of Hormuz has been set back by a lack of regional consensus on the future of the waterway.
Officials from Iran, Iraq and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) nations – minus objecting Bahrain – were scheduled to meet in Oman’s port city of Salalah on Monday to confer on new temporary routes in the Strait of Hormuz amid Tehran’s ongoing hot-and-cold war with the United States.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Red Sea nations watch as Houthis seize Bab al-Mandeb strait
- list 2 of 4Trump tells Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian diesel supplies
- list 3 of 4Tehran and Muscat delay talks, citing regional consensus need
- list 4 of 4Yemen gov’t forces advance in Taiz as Houthis claim attack on Saudi Arabia
On Sunday night, the region’s officials announced the postponement of the meeting, without giving a new date. None of the stakeholders gave any indication that the postponement was directly linked to recent Houthi and Iraqi militia attacks on Saudi Arabia.
However, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Saudi objection was the reason for the postponement, without providing further details.
US media outlets Axios and CNN reported that Saudi Arabia had submitted amendments to the Iran-Oman proposal for Hormuz because it had concerns that the wording would establish a new status quo which would be unacceptable to Riyadh.
It comes days after Saudi Arabia shut down its critical East-West oil pipeline – the kingdom’s key route for energy exports – after drone attacks in the area originating from Iraq. US President Donald Trump said these attacks were likely conducted at Tehran’s behest.
Saudi Arabia has also faced repeated attacks by the Houthis, who took control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast over the weekend.
Hours after the Salalah meeting was postponed, the Saudi civil defence issued alerts for Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran in southern and western parts of the kingdom. The Houthis claimed to have fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at military facilities in Khamis Mushait, in retaliation for air strikes across Yemen, which it blames on Saudi Arabia.
What comes next?
Iran has said it will engage with the US on the future of the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war only if there are tangible moves to lift Washington’s naval blockade on the country and return to the June memorandum of understanding.
With continued disruptions to the passage of vessels through the strait, Iran has signalled that it intends to continue pursuing the bilateral agreement with Oman over Hormuz, which it said was finalised last month.
“In consultation with Oman, in the next step, we will make a decision on how to announce or register the agreement,” Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei told reporters during a weekly news conference on Monday.
When the two countries initially advanced the bilateral deal, Trump threatened to bomb Oman if it “gets in the way” of US talks with Iran.
Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that Tehran wants to use its leverage over Hormuz for regional legitimacy – and ultimately to pressure the US.
“The broader the regional buy-in, the harder it becomes for the US to dismiss the arrangement as an Iranian diktat,” he told Al Jazeera.
GCC states, suffering from a sharp decrease in energy receipts, want ships moving and their economies insulated from a war they neither started nor can end. But Vaez said Washington is unlikely to lift the blockade on Iran even if the region blesses the arrangement between Muscat and Tehran.
“[The US] will find it much harder to sustain a policy that its own partners increasingly see as perpetuating the crisis,” Vaez said
Temporary entry and exit
The Omani-Iranian planned agreement envisions temporary entry and exit routes for commercial vessels in the strait, with Tehran repeatedly stating that this would not mean that the Strait of Hormuz has reopened.
Iran and Oman are the only two countries with territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz. The proposed inbound corridor reportedly goes through Iranian waters, while the outbound corridor mostly passes through Omani waters, with small parts still in Iranian territory.
During Monday’s scheduled meeting, Iran and Oman were supposed to share precise maps and discuss the details of the routes with GCC members Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Kuwait, and Iraq, which is outside the bloc. The deal could reportedly include voluntary tolls to fund navigation, environmental protection and search-and-rescue operations.
Bahrain, which has borne the brunt of Iranian attacks since the US-Israel war on Iran started at the end of February, said it would not participate in the forum since it would amount to “appeasement”. The Tasnim news outlet, affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), claimed Israel pushed Bahrain to refuse participation.
How does Yemen fit in this picture?
The latest diplomatic movement comes after days of explosive developments in Yemen, when the Houthis, officially known as Ansar Allah, essentially took control of the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the Red Sea after a lightning offensive against government forces.
Thomas Juneau, assistant professor in the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa, said the Houthi advances represent a significant gain for Iran. Its Yemeni allies’ position in the Red Sea offers Iran an important new bargaining chip in future negotiations with the US.
“The Houthis are not a simple arm of Iranian foreign policy. They operate largely based on their own interests, and do not take and execute Iranian commands,” he told Al Jazeera. “But Houthi and Iranian interests are largely, if not always fully, aligned. They cooperate closely on the basis of those shared interests.”
Juneau sees the ability for Iran and the Houthis to potentially partially block traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb – two of the world’s most crucial maritime bottlenecks – would give them tremendous influence over the global economy, and thus the US.
The Houthis are trying to seize the opportunity to “institutionalise the de facto reality of their veto on maritime traffic” in the southern Red Sea and replicate partial Iranian success in doing the same in the Strait of Hormuz, Juneau said.
Iran has stressed that their allies’ gains in the Red Sea cannot be separated from the Saudi-led blockade and attacks on Houthi areas in Yemen since 2015.
“We know very well that continued war between Islamic countries in the region only has one winner, and that winner is no one but the Zionist regime, which is after persisting tensions and conflict in our region and between Islamic countries,” Iranian spokesperson Baghaei said.
news.summary: Iran and Oman are the only two countries with territorial waters in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has stressed that their allies’ gains in the Red Sea cannot be separated from the Saudi-led blockade and attacks on Houthi areas in Yemen since 2015.

news.title: Stock futures fall as investors weigh calls for AI slowdown, oil gains: Live updates
news.raw_text:
Stocks fell on Monday as investors monitored a major shakeup in the pipeline for artificial intelligence initial public offerings amid growing safety concerns as well as the latest moves in Treasury yields and oil.
Global AI-related stocks fell after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown of the development of AI capabilities, with other major tech figures backing the proposal.
Amodei said in an essay on Saturday that AI companies need to slow the pace of innovation for their best models due to safety risks, and told CBS News on Sunday that the "toughest dilemma" about such a proposal is what would happen if China did not do the same.
"Obviously some high profile names stating that the acceleration of Frontier AI models needs to slow may be a sticker shock, but, in a way, this feels exactly what the markets want," said David Wagner, head of equity at Aptus Capital Advisors. "If capex spend were to slow, so would earnings, but free-cash-flow would likely inflect higher, which could create multiple expansion back to levels witnessed in December 2025."
"Nonetheless, the market knows it's entering a seasonally weak period. Coupled with a lot of mid-term rhetoric, this could create an environment where stocks continue to take a breather," he added.
U.S. crude prices broke above $100 per barrel last week for the first time since May amid an escalation of conflict in the Middle East.
Last week's rally in oil prices dragged on the three major stock averages. The Dow slid 1.6%, marking its biggest weekly loss since March. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite shed about 0.8% and 0.7%, respectively.
The Federal Reserve gathers for its September policy meeting this week. Fed funds futures traders are pricing in a roughly 90% likelihood of a rate hike, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
Treasury yields spiked ahead of the meeting, with the 10-year yield hitting its highest level since October 2023 on Monday. The yield was last up more than 3 basis points at 5.012%.
11 Min Ago
Trump pushes back against calls for more AI regulation
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to the media before boarding Air Force One for a trip to the Republican National Midterm Convention, at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, U.S. September 9, 2026.
Evan Vucci | Reuters
President Donald Trump on Monday pushed back against growing calls for greater regulation of artificial intelligence, and lashed out at Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei over his urgent plea for an AI slowdown.
"The only control or 'guardrails' that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!" Trump wrote in a Truth Social post.
"The Trump Administration has stopped AI 'people' from doing bad, or potentially bad, 'things,' like Dario (Anthropic!), who is now pretending to be a 'perfect little angel' - and we will continue to do so!" Trump wrote.
10-year Treasury yield hits 5% for first time since 2023
The 10-year U.S. Treasury note yield rose to a multiyear high on Monday ahead of this week's Federal Reserve interest rate decision.
The benchmark rate — which influences mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was up more than 2 basis points at 5%, the highest level since October 2023.
Bitcoin is heading into an important week, with a key procedural Clarity Act vote and the Federal Reserve's upcoming policy decision both capable of shifting the market's next move.
The price of bitcoin has held up in recent weeks despite hotter U.S. inflation, rising oil prices and a hawkish repricing of Fed rate expectations. After a sharp rally last month – when bitcoin posted its biggest three-day gain and strongest week since 2023, pulling it out of a months-long slump – it has since stalled below $80,000.
The crypto market structure bill known as the Clarity Act could provide an upside catalyst if it advances out of Tuesday's Senate vote. But even a positive outcome could bring profit-taking as attention shifts back to the Fed's rate decision, due Wednesday. The FOMC decision could be just as important for bitcoin – a more hawkish stance could push yields and the dollar higher and put pressure on risk assets, while a dovish signal could provide some relief. A failed Clarity vote, meanwhile, could also trigger a selloff given the legislation's importance to the crypto industry.
"While this move has earned our respect, momentum is starting to roll as price has stalled below $80,000 for over two weeks," Wolfe Research said of bitcoin, adding that after its recent move higher it has "plenty room left to run further once this overbought condition subsides."
Wolfe sees $82,000 as the resistance level to watch and $76,000 as key support.
— Tanaya Macheel
2 Hours Ago
Stocks open lower
The three major averages kicked off the week in negative territory.
The S&P 500 fell 0.7% just after 9:30 a.m., while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.2%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 140 points, or 0.3%.
— Sean Conlon
3 Hours Ago
Brent crude tops $109
Vantor satellite image shows fire damage and extensive blackened areas in and around the East-West pipeline pumping station in Saudi Arabia following the September 11, 2026 drone attack and resulting fires.
Maxar | Maxar | Getty Images
Crude oil prices popped on Monday after Saudi Arabia closed its critical pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were up 4.7% to $104.72 per barrel by 8:41 a.m. ET. Brent crude, the international benchmark, traded 4.7% higher to $109.56 per barrel. Prices gained about 9% last week as fighting escalated between the U.S. and Iran. Read more.
Consumer prices rose 3.4% in August from a year earlier, while average hourly earnings increased 3.1%, the weakest wage growth since May 2021.
Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told CNBC that April marked the turning point after a lengthy stretch in which wage growth generally exceeded inflation.
A prolonged squeeze on purchasing power is already starting to show up in consumer spending. More shoppers are shifting toward warehouse clubs and discount retailers.
"People who used to shop at Whole Foods are now at Costco, Aldi, and so you can see that people are still really trying to stretch every dollar," Long said, adding that the behavior is appearing "almost across the income spectrum."
"The frustration is real on inflation and affordability," she said.
— Deena Zaidi
4 Hours Ago
Intel, Diamondback Energy and Palo Alto Networks among the stocks making moves before the bell
Check out the companies making the biggest moves premarket:
Chip stocks — Major chip stocks fell in premarket trading after leaders within the artificial intelligence space, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, called for a slowdown in the development of AI capabilities. Intel slid nearly 6%, Marvell Technology fell over 7.4% and Advanced Micro Devices slipped over 5%.
Cybersecurity stocks — The group rose broadly as worries around AI safety increased following the warnings from CEOs Elon Musk, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman that the technology was moving too fast. Palo Alto Networks traded more than 4% higher, while CrowdStrike advanced 5.4%.
Gold, silver prices fall as traders look ahead to Fed rates decision
Argor-Heraeus' CEO Robin Kolvenbach holds one kilo bars of silver and gold at the plant of refiner and bar manufacturer Argor-Heraeus in Mendrisio, Switzerland, July 13, 2022.
Denis Balibouse | Reuters
Precious metals prices are lower in early trading as traders look ahead to the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision due later in the week.
Spot silver is down more than 3% to $62.54/oz, while spot gold is down by around 1% to $4,306.19/oz.
7 Hours Ago
OpenAI boss Sam Altman spells out how and why the AI industry wants to slow down: ‘We could lose control’
OpenAi founder Sam Altman speaks during the G20 Innovation Ministerial on September 2, 2026 in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Tech leaders from around the world gathered in Chapel Hill for two days of the annual meeting before the G20 Summit.
Sean Rayford | Getty Images
OpenAI chief Sam Altman has made his most detailed comments yet on how AI safety frameworks could work, after he joined Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Elon Musk in warning the industry needs to slow down.
"We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI," Altman said in a post on X just after midnight on Monday, adding that "no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness."
Altman warned of two ways AI progress could go "very badly", including losing "control of the future to AI" and too much power concentrating around a single person or company.
AI stocks slide after major CEOs unite to urge slowdown
Dario Amodei, co-founder and chief executive officer of Anthropic, during a Bloomberg Television interview in San Francisco, California, US, on Tuesday, Dec. 9, 2025.
David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images
Global AI-related stocks fell on Monday after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown of the development of AI capabilities, with other major tech figures backing the proposal.
In Asia, South Korean heavyweights SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics closed down more than 6% and 4%, respectively. Shares of SoftBank, one of the biggest investors in OpenAI, fell 10% in Japan.
In Europe, semiconductor and other AI-related stocks also fell sharply in early trading. Chip equipment giant ASML fell more than 4%, Nokia was down around 5% and Infineon dropped more than 6%. Other companies with business ties to the buildout of data centers, such as Siemens Energy and Schneider Electric, were also lower.
Novo Nordisk stock jumps after drugmaker announces rebrand
Novo Nordisk stock rose 1.3% in morning trading after the Danish company announced a rebranding and said it will go by the name "Novo" going forward.
The Danish drugmaker called the changes the beginning of a new chapter, as it faces stiff competition from Eli Lilly and investor pressure to deliver new blockbuster products.
In a release, Novo also announced a broader company rebrand focused around the phrase "Lasting Health Starts Now," which promotes the idea that patients should make progress toward long-term well-being immediately rather than later.
Coming into Monday trading, Novo's Copenhagen-listed shares were down 14% year-to-date.
Read more from CNBC's Annika Kim Constantino here.
8 Hours Ago
Asia-Pacific markets mixed amid concerns over Mideast tensions
Japan's Nikkei 225 closed 0.81% lower at 63,492.99, while South Korea's Kospi fell 3.26% to 6,684.37.
Australia's benchmark S&P/ASX 200 inched 0.10% higher at 8,749.90.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng index was up 0.39% in the last hour of trade on Monday, while mainland China's CSI 300 closed 0.67% lower at 4,480.08.
— Justina Lee
8 Hours Ago
AstraZeneca shares rise despite trial miss
AstraZeneca Plc signage at the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York, US, on Friday, June 5, 2026.
Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images
AstraZeneca's London-listed shares rose 1.5% in early Monday trading after the drugmaker said its breast cancer pill failed to improve progression-free survival in a late-stage trial.
The drug, camizestrant, sold as Etcamah, showed a numerical but not statistically significant improvement when tested in combination with Pfizer's cancer medicine Palbociclib (sold as Ibrance), AstraZeneca said late Friday.
The company said it would share further data in "due course."
RBC analysts called the result a "manageable setback" that had been largely expected after a trial failure by Swiss peer Roche for a similar drug tempered investor expectations earlier this year.
Citi analysts said AstraZeneca's latest miss had limited downside, as it was offset by a trial win for the same drug in another study that showed camizestrant benefited a more specific group of cancer patients, a treatment for which the drug has already gained approval.
"Data may act as a clearing event for investors looking to Buy AZN at its attractive valuation (14x 27E) for 2H26/FY27 catalysts," Citi said. The stock is down 15% year-to-date.
AstraZeneca is expected to release results from the closely watched AVANZAR trial for lung cancer during the second half of 2026.
— Elsa Ohlen
9 Hours Ago
European stocks open lower as oil prices soar
European stocks dropped in early trading in London, with most regional bourses in the red.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 index fell 0.15% in early trade.
Germany's DAX was down 0.3% shortly after the bell, while France's CAC 40 fell 0.4%.
Italy's FTSE MIB dropped 0.5%, and Spain's IBEX fell 0.2%.
The U.K.'s FTSE 100 was trading 0.4% higher, helped by rising oil majors BP and Shell, both up around 1.5% on the back of rising oil prices.
— Elsa Ohlen
9 Hours Ago
CNBC Daily Open: ‘Whoever wins AI, wins’
Most days, they are arch rivals looking to gain an edge on one another in the most significant space since the Internet.
But in a rare moment, the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI have come together to support the view that the development of AI models should slow down amid growing fears over the technology's capacity to cause harm.
However, President Donald Trump seems to have little desire to cede America's place in the AI race.
Shein shares fall 10% amid urgent recall of contact-lens cleaner by Australia, New Zealand
A woman looks at her smartphone while walking past a SHEIN sign outside the company's office on July 14, 2026, in Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, China.
Cheng Xin | Getty Images
Shares of fast-fashion company Shein fell as much as 10% in Hong Kong, amid news that one of its contact lens products has been recalled by Australia and New Zealand.
"A sample of these contact lenses tested positive for Burkholderia cepacia complex, a bacterial contaminant detected in the solution in which the lenses were packaged," according to a statement by New Zealand's Ministry of Business, Innovation & Employment on Friday.
"Exposure to this bacterium may pose a risk of eye infection or irritation and an incident was reported in the United Kingdom involving a user who developed an eye infection," it added.
The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission issued a similar recall.
— Justina Lee
12 Hours Ago
Z.ai shares tumble over 10% after $5 billion fundraising, its second major raise in two months
Matteo Della Torre | Nurphoto | Getty Images
Shares of Chinese artificial intelligence company Z.ai tumbled more than 10% on Monday after the company announced plans to raise about $5 billion through a new share placement and convertible bond sale, marking its second major fundraising in two months.
The Beijing-based company plans to issue up to 21.97 million new shares at HK$714 each, raising gross proceeds of about HK$15.68 billion ($2 billion). The placement price represents a 10% discount to Z.ai's Friday closing price of HK$793.
Separately, Z.ai plans to issue 20.14 billion yuan ($3 billion) in zero-coupon convertible bonds due in 2027. The bonds will initially be convertible at HK$892.50 per share, a 12.5% premium to Friday's closing price.
— Jenny Lee

France’s hottest summer ever is hitting winemakers right in the grapes, making it harder to produce Champagne that meets the strict classification regulations set by French authorities. Growing ’pagne: Thanks to record temperatures and drought, grape growers had to harvest their crop earlier than ever, leaving them with a fruit that had way higher sugar levels than normal. ai_security.title: Evolving With Agentic Risk: Updating Our Integrated AI Security & Safety Framework
ai_security.summary: Screenshot of updated OB-001 Goal Hijacking techniques A new objective: OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures The larger change is a new objective, OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures. We classify this as AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency: the agent exceeded its authority and ignored a stop condition without an attacker or exploit.
ai_security.raw_text:
With research and development assistance from Konstantin Berlin, Edmund Dyer-Essig, Andy Hsu, and Karthick Kalyanasundaram
Nine months ago, we introduced the Integrated AI Safety and Security Framework as a unified and comprehensive taxonomy to help organizations identify and mitigate the security and safety risks unique to AI systems. Existing frameworks remained essential, but they didn’t fully capture how AI could be manipulated, produce harmful outputs, or take unexpected actions. This left security teams and executives without a common language for planning defenses or explaining AI risk across the business. You can browse the taxonomy here.
Our v1 taxonomy denoted the scenarios where threats applied to agentic systems, which helped teams distinguish risks relevant to autonomous systems rather than to a single prompt-and-response exchange. In the months since, our understanding of how agentic systems fail has evolved alongside their accelerated adoption. Agents now plan, call tools, run code, move money, and delegate work to other agents across long, multi-step tasks. That autonomy creates risks beyond a bad output: an agent can widen its own permissions, replace its goal, or game the metric used to judge success. Even recently, we’ve witnessed these failures occur, as more developments continue to unfold.
We are excited to release v2 of our taxonomy, including the introduction of a new objective: Agentic Autonomy Failures, with three new Techniques and eight new Subtechniques. This update gives organizations a shared, actionable framework for setting boundaries, designing controls, evaluating agent behavior, and aligning security, governance, research, and policy before agents reach consequential systems.
Merging prompt injection and jailbreak
In v1, OB-001 Goal Hijacking, which covered prompt injection, and OB-002 Jailbreak, were separate objectives. In practice, the distinction was difficult to apply.
Ask five researchers to classify the hardest adversarial attacks as prompt injection or jailbreak, and the answers will likely differ. Many of the same adversarial techniques can be applied to both types of attacks, especially as they involve inputs redirecting model behavior away from intended instructions or constraints, even though the source of that input and the appropriate defenses may differ. This ambiguity can force detectors to separate heavily overlapping categories, degrading label quality and making detection less reliable.
Goal Hijacking now covers both, while lower-level techniques preserve distinctions that matter, including input source and defenses. The structure better reflects how attacks work without discarding operational detail.
Figure 1. Screenshot of updated OB-001 Goal Hijacking techniques
A new objective: OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures
The larger change is a new objective, OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures. Goal Hijacking covers external direction; this objective covers an agent diverging without an identifiable external instruction. These failures can emerge when a capable agent receives real autonomy. We group them three ways:
- AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency: The agent acts beyond the authority it was given, skipping an approval it was supposed to wait for, or reaching for a tool, permission, or resource outside the task at hand.
- AITech-2.2 Goal Drift: The agent changes course on its own, quietly adding unauthorized work, substituting a different goal for the one it was asked to pursue, or eroding its own constraints and stop conditions over a long session.
- AITech-2.3: Reward Hacking: The agent optimizes for the appearance of success, gaming a metric, working around a check meant to verify its work, or taking a shortcut it was told not to.
These failure modes are no longer theoretical: in July 2025, an AI coding agent deleted a live production database during an explicit code freeze, after being instructed repeatedly not to make changes, and then wrongly reported that the deletion could not be rolled back. We classify this as AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency: the agent exceeded its authority and ignored a stop condition without an attacker or exploit.
Agentic failures can also compound across runs and systems. In July 2026, OpenAI reported that agents operating with reduced safeguard coordinated through an unauthorized message board, circumvented network controls, and compromised part of Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. Independent reviewers found that many agents recognized the activity was out of scope, but continued pursuing ways to influence the ExploitGym scorer. Humans set the objective, but the agents coordinated and chained the actions autonomously. The incident combined AITech-2.3 Reward Hacking with actions that exceeded the intended evaluation boundary (AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency).
Goal Drift requires a materially different objective without an identifiable external instruction. If a user, attacker, tool response, or poisoned document introduces the new direction, we track the behavior under OB-001 Goal Hijacking. Separating “the agent drifted on its own” from “something pushed it” matters for attribution and defense, because the controls you would build for each are different.
We expect this objective to grow in importance, especially as agents take on more consequential work with less human oversight. These failures can turn a helpful assistant into an incident, and likely not even trigger a content safety guardrail.
Figure 2. Screenshot of new OB-002 Agent Autonomy Failures techniques and subtechniques
Turning definitions into decisions
A taxonomy that names categories provides vocabulary, but we have also authored constitutions to operationalize our AI Security Framework. The constitutions provide per-category specifications define scope, resolve hard cases, distinguish neighboring categories, and provide examples on both sides of the line.
We’ve written before about why this approach matters: No human annotator can hold a definition detailed enough to resolve every borderline case in working memory. A frontier model can apply the full specification to each decision. The written definition therefore becomes a consistent reference for detection, retraining, customer explanations, and compliance review.
As agents become more capable, organizations will give them more autonomy, and the consequences of going off course will grow. The challenge is to supervise them without neutralizing the autonomy that makes them useful. Our constitutions for Excessive Agency, Goal Drift, and Reward Hacking are designed around that tension. They evaluate the full trajectory, not a single message, and distinguish a brief deviation the agent corrects on its own from behavior that continues toward or results in harm. User intervention does not count as self-correction. A verified rollback may clear the outcome-based label if it fully restores the intended state, but it does not erase an authorization violation or security event from audit and incident telemetry.
What this means for you
- If you build or deploy agents: treat Agentic Autonomy Failures as a design and evaluation checklist. Relevant controls could include least-privilege tool access, explicit approval gates for consequential actions, immutable task and stop conditions, independent outcome verification, bounded execution and network access, and complete audit trails across messages, tool calls, and resulting state changes.
- If you lead AI risk or governance: define autonomy tiers, accountable owners, approval boundaries, and evidence requirements before agents receive access to consequential systems.
- If you work in AI security or safety: use the taxonomy as a shared reference for connecting research findings, security controls, evaluations, and policy. Mapping work to common categories makes it easier to compare results across organizations, identify gaps, and build a robust AI security program.
What’s next
The framework is meant to evolve as the threat landscape does, and right now the landscape is moving fastest around autonomy. We’re sharing this update to get it in front of the practitioners living these problems. Feedback, counterexamples, and disagreement are all genuinely welcome.

ai_security.title: Hackers Use Autonomous AI Agents to Launch Mass Credential Theft Attacks in Under 6 Hours
ai_security.summary: A single exposed access token can give attackers a trusted path into cloud services, source code repositories, automation pipelines, and sensitive business data. Organizations should treat AI tool configurations, developer tokens, and cloud API keys as sensitive credentials.
ai_security.raw_text:
Cybercriminals are using autonomous AI agents to turn compromised cloud systems into fast-moving credential theft platforms.
In one recent case, attackers planned, built, and launched a large-scale campaign in less than six hours, stealing thousands of third-party credentials.
The operation shows how attackers can combine AI coding tools, automated scanning, and cloud resources to work at a speed that previously required a larger team and far more time.
Rather than manually checking systems and fixing errors, the agents handled much of the work themselves. Analysts from Google Cloud identified the activity while tracking the growing use of AI-driven automation in real-world intrusions.
Google Cloud said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that the attackers used an AI coding chatbot, a prompt, and preconfigured instructions to carry out the campaign.
The incident is part of a broader shift in cybercrime. Attackers are increasingly using AI to scan for weaknesses, create phishing content, write malicious code, steal secrets, and maintain access after an initial break-in. This trend makes rapid detection and strong cloud security more important than ever.
Hackers Use Autonomous AI Agents
The financially motivated attackers first compromised an organization’s cloud infrastructure, then used it as the launch point for their operation.
Working from a trusted cloud environment helped their traffic appear more legitimate and made it harder for defenders to quickly separate malicious activity from normal services.
The AI-driven framework used written instruction files as operating playbooks. These instructions guided the agents through vulnerability scanning, credential collection, troubleshooting, and IP address rotation without requiring constant human decisions.
The result was a campaign that harvested credentials at a scale normally associated with much larger criminal groups.
This differs from traditional information stealers, which usually wait for a victim to run malicious software and then collect data from that device.
In this case, the agents actively searched server-side systems, identified weaknesses, and carried out targeted actions against online infrastructure.
The campaign highlights the risks outlined in recent reporting on AI agents breach company networks, where automated agents can map services, locate exposed tokens, and move toward valuable administrative access.
Once valid credentials are collected, criminals can reuse them for cloud access, fraud, espionage, extortion, or additional attacks.
Researchers also found an exposed command-and-control server hosting a separate automated reconnaissance and credential management framework called Recon.
Its dashboard was designed to organize, validate, and manage more than 23,800 stolen secrets in real time, including API keys connected to cloud and AI services.
The source report illustrates how attackers combined compromised cloud resources, AI-generated instructions, automated scanning, and credential harvesting into a single accelerated operation.
Cloud and Developer Systems Face Growing Risk
The attack demonstrates why cloud credentials and developer environments have become high-value targets. A single exposed access token can give attackers a trusted path into cloud services, source code repositories, automation pipelines, and sensitive business data.
The risks are similar to those described in stolen cloud credentials attacks, where valid keys can let intruders enter as approved users.
AI coding environments can create additional openings when developers download unsafe packages, clone altered repositories, or allow tools to process untrusted workspace files.
In related activity, the UNC6780 group used compromised developer accounts to distribute trojanized resources and targeted CI/CD environments for authentication tokens.
The DUSTMAKER credential stealer was also observed hiding files inside common AI coding workspace directories.
It could use malicious configuration files to influence an assistant into running scripts during routine development work, while fake pipeline tasks disguised as AI utilities searched for extra tokens and keys.
Organizations should treat AI tool configurations, developer tokens, and cloud API keys as sensitive credentials.
Security teams should rotate exposed keys quickly, apply least-privilege permissions, protect CI/CD runners, review third-party dependencies, and investigate unexpected automation tasks or workspace configuration changes.
Teams should also monitor cloud activity for unusual API calls, unfamiliar service accounts, unexpected public services, and suspicious outbound scanning.
Guidance from coverage of typosquatted npm package theft shows why dependency checks and secret scanning remain essential for development teams.
The findings do not mean autonomous exploitation is now common across every intrusion. However, they show that AI agents can reduce the delay between compromise and credential theft.
Defenders need controls that can detect abuse at the same pace, especially as attackers continue combining AI automation with familiar methods such as stolen credentials, exposed services, and malicious packages.

ai_security.title: AI Agents for Cybersecurity: How Agentic AI Is Changing Threat Detection, Incident Response and the SOC
ai_security.summary: What Are AI Agents for Cybersecurity? They can help with alert investigation, threat intelligence, vulnerability management, phishing analysis, identity security, cloud security, endpoint security, incident response and risk assessment.
ai_security.raw_text:
AI Agents for Cybersecurity: How Agentic AI Is Changing Threat Detection, Incident Response and the SOC
Cybersecurity is entering an important new phase of artificial intelligence.
Security teams already use machine learning, automation and generative AI to identify threats, investigate alerts and analyse large volumes of security data. AI agents take the concept further by enabling systems to reason through investigations, use security tools, coordinate multiple steps and take approved defensive actions.
This is the emerging idea of the agentic Security Operations Center, or agentic SOC.
Instead of simply telling an analyst that something suspicious happened, an AI agent can potentially investigate what happened, collect additional evidence, determine which systems are affected, evaluate the likely threat and recommend or execute an appropriate response within defined permissions.
The timing is significant because defenders are facing increasingly fast and complex attacks. Microsoft Research says agentic AI can help address longstanding cybersecurity bottlenecks by ingesting and reasoning over natural-language and code-based information, including tasks such as supply-chain analysis.
At the same time, attackers are also gaining access to increasingly capable AI systems. Microsoft has warned that autonomous systems can operate continuously while attackers can use AI to increase the speed and scale of offensive operations, creating pressure for defenders to operate at machine speed as well.
That creates a new cybersecurity race:
AI against AI.
What Are AI Agents for Cybersecurity?
AI agents for cybersecurity are AI-powered systems designed to perform security tasks or workflows with some degree of autonomy.
Microsoft describes agentic AI in cybersecurity as the use of autonomous agents to detect, investigate and respond to threats with minimal human intervention.
A cybersecurity agent may potentially:
- monitor security alerts;
- investigate suspicious activity;
- correlate events across systems;
- analyse malware or code;
- search threat intelligence;
- identify affected assets;
- recommend containment actions;
- create incident reports;
- update security systems;
- carry out approved remediation.
The central difference from a conventional AI assistant is action within a security workflow.
A chatbot might explain what a phishing attack is.
An AI security agent could potentially investigate a suspected phishing incident, identify affected users, search email systems for related messages, determine whether malicious links were accessed and prepare containment actions for approval.
AI Assistants vs. AI Agents in Cybersecurity
The distinction is particularly important inside a Security Operations Center.
| AI assistant | AI agent | 
|---|---|
| Explains alerts | Investigates alerts | 
| Summarizes incidents | Collects and correlates evidence | 
| Suggests commands | Can use approved security tools | 
| Answers analyst questions | Can execute multi-step workflows | 
| Human performs the actions | Agent can perform approved actions | 
| Primarily informational | Operational | 
This does not mean that every security agent should operate without human oversight.
In high-risk environments, the best design may be:
AI investigates → AI recommends → human approves → AI executes
rather than:
AI investigates → AI executes everything
The appropriate level of autonomy depends on the risk of the action.
Why AI Agents Matter for Cybersecurity
Security teams face a fundamental scale problem.
Organizations generate enormous quantities of logs, alerts, network activity, identity events, endpoint signals and cloud telemetry.
Human analysts cannot investigate every signal in the same depth.
This creates a familiar problem:
More data → more alerts → more investigation workload
AI agents potentially change that equation by handling more of the investigative workload.
Microsoft Research notes that many cybersecurity problems remain difficult or inefficient because they require large amounts of human labor. Its 2026 research maps these challenges to emerging agentic AI capabilities and identifies applications across areas including supply-chain security.
The potential advantage is not simply faster analysis.
It is the ability to continuously investigate.
What Is an Agentic SOC?
An agentic SOC is a Security Operations Center in which AI agents participate directly in security operations.
Traditional SOC:
Alert → Analyst → Investigation → Decision → Response
Agentic SOC:
Alert → Agent investigation → Evidence collection → Analysis → Recommendation or approved action → Human oversight
A mature system may eventually involve multiple specialist agents working together.
For example:
Detection Agent → Investigation Agent → Threat Intelligence Agent → Response Agent
A central orchestrator can coordinate the workflow.
Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike are among the vendors actively developing agentic SOC architectures, reflecting a broader industry movement toward AI-driven security operations.
Why the SOC Is Becoming Agentic
Attackers increasingly automate reconnaissance, exploitation and other stages of an attack.
CrowdStrike reported that average eCrime breakout time fell to 29 minutes in 2025, with the fastest observed breakout taking only 27 seconds.
Palo Alto Networks has similarly reported that vulnerability discovery to exploitation can occur in under 25 minutes in its threat research.
These measurements come from security vendors using their own datasets and methodologies, so they should be interpreted as indicators rather than universal measurements of every attack.
The strategic point is nevertheless clear:
A defense process that requires hours of manual investigation can struggle against machine-speed attacks.
Agentic security attempts to narrow that gap.
How AI Agents Work in Cybersecurity
A security agent can be understood through a sequence:
Detect → Investigate → Reason → Decide → Act → Verify
Detection
The system receives a signal.
That might be:
- an endpoint alert;
- unusual authentication;
- suspicious network traffic;
- a malicious file;
- an anomalous cloud event;
- a potential phishing message.
Investigation
The agent gathers additional evidence.
It might search:
- endpoint telemetry;
- identity systems;
- email;
- cloud logs;
- network data;
- threat intelligence;
- vulnerability information.
Reasoning
The agent evaluates the evidence and attempts to determine:
- what happened;
- whether the activity is malicious;
- which assets are involved;
- how serious the event is.
Decision
The agent determines what should happen next according to its instructions and permissions.
Action
Depending on the risk level, it can recommend or perform an approved action.
Verification
A sophisticated workflow should check whether the action produced the intended result.
This final step is important.
An agent should not simply execute an action and assume success.
AI Agents for Threat Detection
Threat detection is one of the most obvious applications.
An agent can potentially monitor large numbers of signals and identify combinations that are difficult for humans to spot manually.
For example:
Unusual login
New device
Privileged account
Suspicious geographic pattern
Abnormal cloud activity
could trigger deeper automated investigation.
The value lies in connecting seemingly separate signals.
Traditional security systems may already correlate events through rules.
AI agents potentially add another layer by interpreting context and adapting the investigation.
AI Agents for Incident Investigation
Incident investigation often consumes substantial analyst time.
An analyst may need to:
- inspect the initial alert;
- identify the affected system;
- search logs;
- examine user activity;
- look for related indicators;
- investigate other systems;
- determine the attack path;
- document the findings.
An AI agent can potentially perform many of these investigative steps automatically.
Instead of presenting the analyst with dozens of disconnected alerts, the agent can produce a structured investigation:
Initial event → Related activity → Affected assets → Attack path → Confidence → Recommended response
The analyst can then review the evidence.
AI Agents for Threat Intelligence
Threat intelligence changes rapidly.
Security teams need to track:
- malware;
- vulnerabilities;
- threat actors;
- indicators of compromise;
- attack techniques;
- campaigns;
- emerging infrastructure.
A threat-intelligence agent can potentially monitor multiple information sources continuously, extract relevant intelligence and connect it with an organization's existing security data.
For example, an agent could identify a newly reported vulnerability and determine:
Which of our systems use the affected software?
That turns external intelligence into an internal security question.
AI Agents for Vulnerability Management
Vulnerability management can involve enormous amounts of information.
Organizations may have thousands of vulnerabilities across servers, endpoints, cloud resources and applications.
The difficult task is often prioritization.
An agent could potentially combine:
- vulnerability severity;
- asset importance;
- exposure;
- exploit availability;
- threat intelligence;
- business context.
Instead of asking:
“Which vulnerabilities have the highest CVSS scores?”
security teams can ask:
“Which vulnerabilities pose the greatest practical risk to our organization right now?”
That is a more meaningful operational question.
AI Agents for Phishing Detection
Phishing remains a major security problem because attackers can target people at scale.
An AI agent could potentially analyse:
- sender information;
- email content;
- links;
- domains;
- attachments;
- historical communications;
- user behaviour.
It could then investigate related messages across the organization.
The agent may also identify whether multiple employees have received variations of the same campaign.
This changes phishing detection from analyzing an individual email to analyzing the campaign behind the emails.
AI Agents for Identity Security
Identity is increasingly central to cybersecurity because attackers can use stolen credentials to access systems without deploying conventional malware.
A security agent can potentially monitor:
- authentication events;
- privilege changes;
- unusual access patterns;
- account activity;
- device changes;
- application access.
It can investigate suspicious identity behaviour and determine whether additional action is warranted.
Microsoft describes identity as a particularly important control plane for securing autonomous AI because agents themselves increasingly operate with credentials and permissions.
That creates an interesting security paradox:
AI agents can improve identity security while simultaneously becoming new identities that must themselves be secured.
AI Agents for Cloud Security
Modern cloud environments can be extremely complex.
Security teams must monitor:
- virtual machines;
- containers;
- APIs;
- identities;
- storage;
- cloud configurations;
- workloads;
- network activity.
An agent can potentially investigate an alert across multiple cloud services and determine whether seemingly minor configuration changes form part of a larger attack pattern.
It may also help security teams identify excessive permissions or exposed resources.
AI Agents for Endpoint Security
Endpoints generate huge quantities of security information.
An AI agent can potentially investigate:
- suspicious processes;
- unusual files;
- persistence mechanisms;
- authentication activity;
- network connections;
- software changes.
A response agent could potentially isolate an affected machine or disable a compromised account when predefined conditions are satisfied.
High-impact actions should generally be governed by explicit policies.
AI Agents for Security Automation
Security automation is not new.
Security orchestration, automation and response platforms have existed for years.
What AI agents potentially add is more flexible reasoning.
Traditional automation might say:
If alert X occurs, execute playbook Y.
An agent can potentially determine:
Given the evidence, which investigation or response should happen next?
This can be useful when every incident does not follow exactly the same sequence.
The goal is not to eliminate automation rules.
It is to combine deterministic automation with more adaptive AI-driven investigation.
Multi-Agent Cybersecurity Systems
Some security problems are too broad for a single agent.
A multi-agent architecture can divide the investigation into specialized roles.
For example:
Detection Agent
Identifies suspicious activity.
Investigation Agent
Collects and correlates evidence.
Threat Intelligence Agent
Checks external intelligence.
Vulnerability Agent
Evaluates affected systems and known vulnerabilities.
Response Agent
Prepares or executes approved containment actions.
Reporting Agent
Documents the investigation.
A coordinator can bring these outputs together.
Microsoft Research has published work on multi-agent cybersecurity architectures that divide risk assessment into stages including organizational profiling, asset mapping, threat analysis, control evaluation, risk scoring and recommendations. Its experimental results show both potential benefits and important limitations, including context-window constraints.
That is a useful lesson:
More agents do not automatically mean better security.
Architecture, context management and reliable coordination matter.
AI Agents for Security Operations Centers
The SOC is where agentic cybersecurity may have its greatest practical impact.
A conventional SOC can be overwhelmed by alert volume.
An agentic SOC can potentially assign AI agents to specific investigative tasks while human analysts supervise the overall process.
CrowdStrike describes its 2026 agentic SOC approach as coordinated multi-agent investigation across endpoint, identity, SaaS, cloud and network domains.
Palo Alto Networks similarly describes agentic SOC architectures designed to combine AI reasoning with security data and automated response workflows.
This points toward a new operating model:
Human analysts + specialized security agents + security platforms
rather than:
Human analysts + dashboards + manual investigation
How AI Agents Can Reduce Alert Fatigue
Alert fatigue occurs when analysts receive more alerts than they can meaningfully investigate.
Agents can potentially help by:
- grouping related alerts;
- suppressing duplicates;
- gathering context;
- prioritizing likely threats;
- explaining why an alert matters;
- investigating low-level signals automatically.
The aim is not simply to reduce the number of alerts.
It is to increase the amount of useful information per alert.
An analyst receiving ten well-investigated incidents may be more effective than an analyst receiving a thousand unexplained alerts.
AI Agents for Security Response
Detection without response is only part of cybersecurity.
An agent can potentially help with containment and remediation.
Possible actions include:
- isolating an endpoint;
- disabling a compromised credential;
- blocking a malicious domain;
- removing malicious email;
- modifying a firewall rule;
- creating a ticket;
- initiating a recovery workflow.
These actions can have significant consequences.
For that reason, many organizations should use approval thresholds.
A possible model is:
Low risk → automatic response
Medium risk → agent recommendation + analyst approval
High risk → human-led response
The Security Risks of AI Agents
AI agents can strengthen cybersecurity while simultaneously creating a new attack surface.
Microsoft's research and security guidance emphasize that agentic systems introduce risks associated with autonomy, tools, permissions and indirect prompt injection.
Prompt Injection
An attacker may try to place malicious instructions inside a webpage, document, email or other data source that an agent processes.
The system must distinguish between data and instructions.
Excessive Permissions
A powerful agent with excessive access can become a serious security risk.
Research from Microsoft identifies over-privileged tools and ambient authority as important risks in cloud-hosted agent environments.
Identity Risk
AI agents increasingly operate using identities and credentials.
Organizations need to know:
Which agent is acting?
On whose behalf?
With which permissions?
For what purpose?
Palo Alto Networks' research similarly identifies identity as a critical control plane for securing autonomous agents.
Data Leakage
Agents may access sensitive information across multiple systems.
Organizations need strict controls around what agents can retrieve and transmit.
Incorrect Actions
An AI agent can misunderstand an incident and execute the wrong response.
The greater the potential impact, the stronger the approval controls should be.
Cascading Failures
One incorrect decision can trigger several additional automated actions.
This makes containment and rollback mechanisms important.
Securing the AI Agents Themselves
Organizations cannot secure an agentic environment only by protecting traditional applications.
The agents themselves become part of the security architecture.
Microsoft recommends applying identity- and policy-based controls to agents and using least-privilege permissions, telemetry and governance.
Important controls include:
Agent identity
Each agent should have an identifiable identity rather than operating as an anonymous automation process.
Least privilege
Agents should have only the permissions they require.
Tool controls
Individual actions and tools should be governed independently where appropriate.
Runtime monitoring
Organizations should be able to observe agent activity.
Approval policies
Sensitive actions should trigger human approval.
Audit trails
Every important action should be traceable.
Isolation
Higher-risk agents may need stronger execution boundaries.
Zero Trust for AI Agents
Traditional Zero Trust principles are becoming increasingly relevant to agentic systems.
The assumption should not be:
“This agent belongs to our organization, so it can be trusted.”
Instead:
Verify → authorize → limit → monitor
An agent should prove what it is and what it is allowed to do.
Microsoft Security has explicitly recommended applying Zero Trust principles to AI agents and treating them as identities that require appropriate access controls.
This could become one of the foundations of enterprise agent security.
AI Agents and the AI-Powered Attacker
Defenders are not the only side adopting AI.
Attackers can potentially use AI systems for:
- reconnaissance;
- phishing;
- vulnerability research;
- social engineering;
- malware development;
- credential attacks;
- target selection;
- automated adaptation.
Microsoft has warned that AI is reducing the cost and increasing the speed of offensive cyber activity.
That creates an uncomfortable reality.
Organizations may need AI agents not because they want more automation, but because defending manually against increasingly automated attackers may become economically unsustainable.
AI Agents for Cyber Risk Assessment
Agentic AI can also be used before an incident occurs.
A security-risk agent could potentially:
- inventory assets;
- map attack surfaces;
- identify vulnerabilities;
- evaluate controls;
- assess threats;
- prioritize risks;
- prepare remediation recommendations.
Microsoft Research published a 2026 multi-agent architecture that performed these stages across simulated organizational environments, demonstrating both the potential and current technical limitations of multi-agent risk assessment.
This could make cybersecurity assessments more accessible to organizations that cannot afford frequent manual assessments.
AI Agents for Supply Chain Security
Modern organizations depend on complex software and technology supply chains.
A security agent could potentially investigate:
- software dependencies;
- vulnerabilities;
- package risks;
- supplier relationships;
- exposed credentials;
- configuration weaknesses.
Microsoft Research specifically identifies supply-chain analysis as an area where agentic AI may help address labor-intensive defensive tasks.
The advantage is scale.
An agent can potentially investigate thousands of dependencies much faster than a human team performing the same work manually.
The Business Case for AI Agents in Cybersecurity
Security leaders ultimately need to justify investment.
Potential benefits include:
Faster investigations
Agents can process evidence and conduct repetitive investigation steps rapidly.
Reduced analyst workload
Security professionals can spend more time on difficult incidents and strategic work.
Improved coverage
Agents can continuously monitor systems that humans cannot manually inspect around the clock.
Faster response
Approved automated actions can reduce the time between detection and containment.
Better consistency
Agents can apply defined investigative procedures repeatedly.
Greater scalability
Security operations can potentially handle increasing volumes of telemetry without adding people at the same rate.
How to Measure the ROI of Security Agents
Cybersecurity organizations should measure outcomes rather than simply counting AI usage.
Important metrics can include:
| Metric | What it measures | 
|---|---|
| Mean time to detect | How quickly threats are identified | 
| Mean time to investigate | How quickly evidence is assembled | 
| Mean time to respond | How quickly action occurs | 
| False-positive rate | Quality of alert prioritization | 
| Analyst workload | Human effort required | 
| Investigation coverage | Percentage of relevant events examined | 
| Automated resolution rate | Share of cases agents resolve successfully | 
| Escalation rate | How often humans must intervene | 
| Cost per incident | Operational efficiency | 
The goal is not maximum automation.
It is better security outcomes at sustainable cost.
How Security Teams Should Deploy AI Agents
The safest approach is gradual.
Start with investigation
Use agents to gather evidence and summarize incidents before giving them response authority.
Add controlled actions
Introduce low-risk automated actions after the investigation workflows prove reliable.
Establish approval thresholds
Define which actions require human review.
Limit permissions
Give each agent only the access necessary for its role.
Test adversarial scenarios
Evaluate prompt injection, malicious data and unusual incidents.
Monitor continuously
Track agent behavior and performance after deployment.
Expand autonomy cautiously
Increase permissions only when evidence shows that the system performs reliably.
The Future of the Security Operations Center
The SOC of the future may look very different from today's analyst-driven model.
Instead of one analyst investigating every alert, a human could supervise a collection of specialized agents.
For example:
Detection Agent
monitors incoming signals.
↓
Investigation Agent
builds the incident timeline.
↓
Threat Intelligence Agent
checks external intelligence.
↓
Identity Agent
investigates compromised accounts.
↓
Endpoint Agent
analyses affected devices.
↓
Response Agent
prepares or executes approved remediation.
↓
Human Analyst
reviews the evidence and makes high-impact decisions.
This is not necessarily science fiction.
Security vendors are already developing agentic SOC products and multi-agent investigation systems.
The remaining question is how much autonomy organizations will trust these systems with.
Human Analysts Will Still Matter
The rise of AI agents does not eliminate the need for cybersecurity professionals.
Instead, the human role can shift.
Security analysts may increasingly focus on:
- complex investigations;
- strategic decisions;
- incident leadership;
- threat hunting;
- system design;
- agent supervision;
- security architecture.
AI can handle scale.
Humans provide context, accountability and judgment.
This distinction becomes particularly important during major incidents where technical information may be incomplete and business consequences are difficult to quantify.
The Future of AI Agents for Cybersecurity
The long-term direction is toward security systems that can perceive, reason and act continuously.
Microsoft's 2026 security strategy describes this as a new cyber stack capable of continuously perceiving risk, reasoning across large amounts of context and taking action at machine speed.
The emerging model can therefore be summarized as:
Sense → Understand → Investigate → Decide → Act → Verify
The challenge is making every stage trustworthy.
An agent that investigates faster but reaches unreliable conclusions is not necessarily better.
An agent that can act faster but has excessive privileges may increase risk.
The future of cybersecurity will therefore depend not only on how capable AI agents become, but also on how effectively organizations control them.
Frequently Asked Questions About AI Agents for Cybersecurity
What are AI agents for cybersecurity?
AI agents for cybersecurity are AI-powered systems that can detect, investigate, analyse and potentially respond to security threats through multi-step workflows.
What is an agentic SOC?
An agentic SOC is a Security Operations Center that uses AI agents to perform or coordinate security investigations and response activities, with humans retaining appropriate oversight.
How can AI agents help cybersecurity teams?
They can help with alert investigation, threat intelligence, vulnerability management, phishing analysis, identity security, cloud security, endpoint security, incident response and risk assessment.
Can AI agents respond to cyberattacks?
They can potentially perform approved defensive actions such as isolating systems, blocking malicious activity or disabling compromised credentials. The appropriate level of autonomy depends on the risk and controls in place.
Can AI agents replace cybersecurity analysts?
They are more likely to change the work of security analysts than eliminate the profession. Agents can handle large volumes of repetitive investigation while humans focus on complex decisions, strategy and accountability.
What is the biggest risk of AI agents in cybersecurity?
One of the biggest risks is giving an autonomous system excessive access to sensitive systems and tools. Prompt injection, incorrect decisions, identity risks and cascading failures are also important concerns.
How do you secure an AI agent?
Important controls include strong identity, least-privilege permissions, tool restrictions, monitoring, audit logs, isolation, testing and human approval for high-impact actions.
What is AI-powered cybersecurity?
AI-powered cybersecurity is the broader use of artificial intelligence to detect, investigate, prevent and respond to cyber threats. Agentic AI adds greater autonomy and multi-step execution.
Are AI agents being used in Security Operations Centers?
Yes. Security vendors are already developing and deploying agentic SOC capabilities, including systems designed to investigate incidents across endpoint, identity, cloud, SaaS and network environments.
Will AI make cyberattacks faster?
AI can potentially reduce the time and expertise required for parts of offensive cyber activity. Security researchers and vendors are therefore increasingly focused on defending against AI-accelerated attacks.
Conclusion
AI agents are changing cybersecurity from a largely alert-driven discipline toward a more continuous, investigative and increasingly autonomous model.
They can potentially collect evidence, investigate incidents, analyse threats, monitor identities, assess vulnerabilities and execute approved responses.
Their greatest advantage may be speed.
Cyberattacks can evolve quickly, and human analysts cannot manually investigate every signal generated by modern digital environments.
Agentic cybersecurity offers a way to increase defensive capacity by allowing AI systems to handle more of the investigative workload.
But autonomy also creates a new security problem.
The defenders' AI must itself be secured.
Agents require identities, permissions, monitoring and governance. They must be protected against prompt injection, excessive privileges, compromised tools and incorrect actions.
The future is therefore unlikely to be:
Humans replaced by AI.
It is more likely to be:
Human security professionals + specialized AI agents + governed automation.
The organizations that get this balance right could gain a significant defensive advantage.
The goal is not to give AI unlimited control.
It is to make AI capable of seeing more, investigating faster and acting safely, while keeping human judgment at the points where it matters most.

ai_security.title: Hackers Weaponize AI Safety Guardrails to Hide Malware From LLM-Powered Security Scanners
ai_security.summary: ESET Researchers have identified a technique called GuardBreaker, that attempts to exploit AI safety guardrails and prevent an LLM-assisted scanner from reaching the malicious portion of a file.
ai_security.raw_text:
Threat actors are adapting malware not only for conventional endpoint defenses and sandboxes, but also for large language model-powered tools increasingly used to triage suspicious code.
ESET researchers linked the activity to Russia-aligned threat actor UAC-0099, which used the method during an attack against an organization in Ukraine.
The group inserted a safety-sensitive, weapon-related request into a comment inside a malicious VBScript file.
Since comments are ignored during normal script execution, the text did not alter the malware’s runtime behavior.
Its intended target was the analysis layer: an LLM that may interpret the embedded text as an instruction rather than inert, attacker-controlled content.
The apparent objective was to trigger a model refusal or otherwise derail the scanner before it inspected the code that followed.
The VBScript was designed to download and install MATCHBOIL, a C#-based loader associated with UAC-0099 that can retrieve follow-on payloads.
Public reporting does not identify a specific affected LLM product, nor does it establish a measured success rate for the technique; the evidence shows the adversarial comment and ESET’s assessment of its intended purpose.
GuardBreaker illustrates a form of indirect prompt injection. In this scenario, the attacker does not send a malicious prompt directly to an AI assistant.
Instead, the hostile instruction is embedded in a file, package, comment, string, or metadata field that an automated security workflow later feeds into an LLM.
The attack exploits a fundamental design challenge in many LLM applications: instructions and untrusted data are handled in the same language-processing context, without a dependable security boundary between them.
OWASP warns that external material, including code comments and documentation, must be treated as untrusted content, sanitized before analysis, and clearly separated from system instructions.
The practical risk is not that a code comment compromises an endpoint by itself. Rather, it can influence the AI component of a detection pipeline.
If a scanner treats an LLM refusal, truncated response, or incomplete analysis as a benign verdict, attackers may gain a blind spot without having to defeat signatures, behavioral detection, or sandbox execution.
ESET Researchers have identified a technique called GuardBreaker, that attempts to exploit AI safety guardrails and prevent an LLM-assisted scanner from reaching the malicious portion of a file.
AI Safety Guardrails
UAC-0099 has a history of targeting Ukrainian government, defense, transportation, and energy-related entities using phishing-led delivery chains.
CERT-UA and other researchers have previously documented the group’s use of MATCHBOIL, MATCHWOK, and DRAGSTARE malware families.
MATCHBOIL can profile infected hosts and retrieve additional components from command-and-control infrastructure.
The GuardBreaker discovery aligns with similar techniques observed in malicious open-source packages.
Researchers have found PyPI and npm packages containing fabricated “system” instructions, text telling AI models to classify the package as clean, and excessive repeated strings intended to consume a model’s context window before it reaches the payload.
This creates several opportunities for adversaries. Malicious code can be placed after a large volume of filler text, hidden inside comments described as confidential data, or stored in unusual file formats that automated workflows parse only partially.
AI agents that can invoke unpackers, deobfuscators, repositories, or external tools also introduce additional risk if prompt-injected content can steer those actions.
Organizations should avoid assigning a single LLM the authority to declare a sample safe.
Security teams should correlate AI-assisted analysis with static signatures, sandbox telemetry, EDR signals, reputation data, detonation results, and analyst review.
An LLM can assist analysts by explaining code, clustering artifacts, or prioritizing suspicious behavior, but it should not replace deterministic inspection and human validation.
A resilient workflow should classify every scanned artifact including comments, strings, filenames, package metadata, and embedded documents as untrusted input.
It should preserve strict boundaries between model instructions and sample content, detect encoding and context-flooding attempts, and route incomplete or refused analyses for further inspection.
OWASP specifically recommends structured prompts, input sanitization, output monitoring, least-privilege tool access, and logging of LLM interactions and agent behavior. Most importantly, a refusal is not a clean verdict.
GuardBreaker demonstrates that as defenders add AI to malware-analysis pipelines, attackers will increasingly treat the model itself and its safety controls as another surface to evade.

ai_security.title: SAS: Simple Attention Sparsification via End-to-End Optimization of Context Ranking
ai_security.abstract: Post-training attention sparsification reduces the quadratic cumulative attention cost of pretrained Transformers by selecting a small set of context units (tokens or blocks) for each query. Existing trainable methods usually use a lightweight selector to score context units, followed by hard Top-K selection that blocks gradients from the language modeling loss. Consequently, these methods commonly distill layer-wise dense attention distributions. Although this encourages the selector to rank context units by dense attention weights in the original model, the ranking is not directly aligned with their impact on predictions under a fixed attention budget (i.e., the number of attended context units per query), potentially wasting the limited budget on less useful units. To address this misalignment, we propose Simple Attention Sparsification (SAS), a gated sparse attention mechanism that optimizes context ranking end-to-end with the language modeling loss. The key idea is to inject the selector's continuous scores into attention logits during training, allowing the loss to update the selector through standard backpropagation. We identify several choices crucial for this simple design to work well in practice: placing the gate inside the attention softmax in log form, using normalized softmax gates to calibrate historical context against the always-retained current block, and preserving continuous selector scores so the model learns relative priorities rather than only hard selections. To support long-sequence training, we implement a memory-efficient Triton kernel that integrates SAS into FlashAttention-style computation. Across reasoning, long-context understanding, and agentic tasks, SAS consistently outperforms trainable sparse attention baselines across attention budgets, with especially large gains under tight budgets, demonstrating more effective context ranking for downstream tasks.
